claims.text: High configurational entropy stabilizes single-phase solid solutions in nearly equiatomic, five-component high-entropy alloys.
Surface-energy minimization drives phase segregation in five-component high-entropy alloy nanoparticles at elevated temperatures.
Below a critical particle diameter, surface energy dominates bulk configurational entropy.
Particles below the critical diameter transform from a single-phase solid solution into a core-shell or multiphase structure.
The nanoparticle transformation deviates from bulk thermodynamic predictions.
CoCrFeMnNi is an example of a multielement solid solution possessing high configurational entropy.
Sub-10 nm CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles can initially exist as a disordered, single-phase FCC solid solution.
The component with the lowest surface energy preferentially diffuses and segregates to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface segregation lowers the activation barrier for nucleating secondary phases in the particle core.
Surface segregation changes the core composition and can move it outside the single-phase stability region.
A segregation-induced change in core composition can cause spinodal decomposition or nucleation and growth of secondary phases.
Bulk configurational entropy suppresses phase segregation and secondary-phase formation.
Nanoparticles below the critical diameter will phase-separate after annealing while bulk material of the same composition remains single-phase.
Segregation begins at lower temperatures and on shorter timescales in nanoparticles than in bulk alloys.
The segregating species has an anomalously high surface diffusion coefficient.

Traditional alloying concepts and bulk thermodynamic models predict that equiatomic alloys with five or more components remain single-phase up to melting when mixing-enthalpy penalties are insignificant.
Particles above the critical diameter are stabilized because the bulk entropy contribution dominates the surface-energy contribution.
Nearly identical component surface energies prevent significant surface segregation.
An initially amorphous or multiphase particle has different structural-evolution driving forces from an initially single-phase particle.
Diffusion in very small clusters may deviate from classical Arrhenius behavior because of nonequilibrium surface states or quantum-size effects.
